cards.title: Two comparisons between transfinite recursion and analytic choice
cards.formal: The source poses two targets: (Q1) is ATR₂′ arithmetically Weihrauch equivalent to ATR₂? (Q2) is analytic choice on Baire space hyperarithmetically Weihrauch reducible to countably parallel analytic choice on ℕ? This inherited record bundles both; no single primary target has yet been selected.
cards.why: Compares the uniform computational content of transfinite recursion and analytic selection, beyond their classification by axioms alone. The distinction between full hierarchies, partial hierarchies and coordinated infinite choices exposes different kinds of effective information.
cards.status_note: Source questions and both early and revised author manuscripts checked; later searches through 11 September 2026 found no matching resolution. No independent proof audit was completed. The bundled target and reduction conventions remain unfinished.

sentences: The source compares two versions of transfinite recursion and two forms of analytic choice.
ATR₂ may return a jump hierarchy for a whole linear order or an infinite decreasing sequence, while ATR₂′ permits a hierarchy on a sufficiently large initial segment.
The first question asks whether those two tasks are equivalent using arithmetical transformations.
The second asks whether hyperarithmetical transformations reduce choice of an infinite sequence to countably many analytic choices of natural numbers.
The inherited record still bundles these distinct targets, and a proved separation for ordinary computable transformations does not resolve the stronger comparison.

cards.definitions: A countable linear order L may be encoded by its domain D⊆ℕ and order relation <_L. It is well-founded when it has no infinite strictly decreasing sequence. Its well-founded part is its largest well-founded initial segment. In the cited preprint, a jump hierarchy is a sequence of sets H_p⊆ℕ satisfying H_p=⊕_{q<_L p}H_q′, where A′ is the halting set for machines with oracle A and ⊕ codes a sequence of sets as one set using pairs of natural numbers. ATR₂ takes a countable linear order and may output either a jump hierarchy on all of it or an infinite decreasing sequence. ATR₂′ permits the hierarchy to be restricted to an initial segment containing the whole well-founded part; it still permits a decreasing sequence instead. Baire space ℕ^ℕ is the space of infinite sequences of natural numbers, and Cantor space 2^ℕ consists of binary sequences. Analytic choice takes a code for a nonempty analytic set A and returns a member of A; analytic means a projection of a closed set with an auxiliary Baire-space coordinate. Countably parallel choice on ℕ receives a sequence of nonempty coded analytic subsets A_i⊆ℕ and returns a sequence (a_i) with a_i∈A_i. An ordinary Weihrauch reduction from f to g uses one uniform computable transformation K of an input x into a valid g-instance and another H that turns (x,y) into an f-solution for every y∈g(K(x)). Arithmetical reducibility permits fixed finite-level arithmetic transformations instead. Q2 permits the broader hyperarithmetical transformations, involving effective transfinite rather than merely finite arithmetic computation; their precise uniform representation remains part of the unfinished final formulation.
cards.answer_criterion: For Q1, establish both arithmetical reductions or prove a failed direction. For Q2, establish the stated hyperarithmetical reduction or its failure. Resolving one does not automatically resolve the other. The record still needs a choice of primary benchmark target and complete conventions for that target; an ordinary computable nonreduction alone does not refute a reduction with stronger preprocessing and postprocessing.

context_blocks.title: Recursion with a second possible output
context_blocks.text: Transfinite recursion usually takes a well-order as a promise. ATR₂ accepts a linear order without that promise and allows an infinite descent as an alternative output. A hierarchy can sometimes exist even on an ill-founded order, so the output is not required to classify the input as well-founded or ill-founded.

context_blocks.title: Full order versus a large initial segment
context_blocks.text: ATR₂′ weakens one output option by allowing a hierarchy on a suitable initial segment. On a well-order, that segment must be the entire order. The distinction therefore lies in ill-founded inputs and how much of their order structure the hierarchy must cover.

context_blocks.title: Independent choices versus a whole infinite object
context_blocks.text: Parallel choice on ℕ selects one number from each separately specified set. Analytic choice on Baire space selects a whole infinite sequence subject to a single analytic condition, which can couple its coordinates. The second question asks whether stronger effective transformations remove the gap between these tasks.

context_blocks.title: A proved ordinary separation leaves stronger reductions open
context_blocks.text: The revised author manuscript proves a separation for computable Weihrauch reductions and then explicitly asks about the hyperarithmetical comparison in Question 3.35. It also retains the arithmetical ATR₂/ATR₂′ comparison as Question 3.37. Theorem 2.12 involves parallelization, so it must not be read as a result for an un-parallelized operator.

cards.context:
Transfinite recursion usually takes a well-order as a promise. ATR₂ accepts a linear order without that promise and allows an infinite descent as an alternative output. A hierarchy can sometimes exist even on an ill-founded order, so the output is not required to classify the input as well-founded or ill-founded.

ATR₂′ weakens one output option by allowing a hierarchy on a suitable initial segment. On a well-order, that segment must be the entire order. The distinction therefore lies in ill-founded inputs and how much of their order structure the hierarchy must cover.

Parallel choice on ℕ selects one number from each separately specified set. Analytic choice on Baire space selects a whole infinite sequence subject to a single analytic condition, which can couple its coordinates. The second question asks whether stronger effective transformations remove the gap between these tasks.

The revised author manuscript proves a separation for computable Weihrauch reductions and then explicitly asks about the hyperarithmetical comparison in Question 3.35. It also retains the arithmetical ATR₂/ATR₂′ comparison as Question 3.37. Theorem 2.12 involves parallelization, so it must not be read as a result for an un-parallelized operator.

methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. We aim for benchmarks of 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. All three use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The possible 1,000-problem expansion has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The targets are 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. Top 100, Top 500 and the possible Top 1000 use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
